name: Jakartan Sign Language
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Palfreyman, Nick. 2017. Sign language varieties of Indonesia: A linguistic and sociolinguistic investigation [dissertation abstract]. Sign Language & Linguistics 20(1). DOI 10.1075/sll.20.1.06pal
sources.note: Nothing on stress; summary of the thesis (negation and completion in Solo and Makassar signing).

sources.citation: Palfreyman, Nick. 2015. Sign language varieties of Indonesia: A linguistic and sociolinguistic investigation. PhD thesis, University of Central Lancashire. 313 pp. (published 2019 as Variation in Indonesian Sign Language: A typological and sociolinguistic analysis. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton / Ishara Press, Sign Language Typology 8, DOI 10.1515/9781501504822, open access)
sources.note: Describes the Solo and Makassar varieties (negation, completion), not Jakarta. The only stress remark is generic, about sign languages as a class (text p. 1, pdf p. 17): 'Even the central properties of prosody – the rhythms, stresses and intonation of speech – are paralleled through the use of non-manual markers (Sandler, 1999; Sandler & Lillo-Martin, 2006; Crasborn, 2006).' Also notes (pdf p. 95) that connected signing is subject to 'phonological and prosodic considerations such as rhythm, stress and intonation (Crasborn, 2006; Sandler, 2012)'. No stress description for any Indonesian variet…

sources.citation: Isma, Silva Tenrisara Pertiwi. 2012. Signing varieties in Jakarta and Yogyakarta: dialects or separate languages? MA thesis, Chinese University of Hong Kong. 90 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent. Chapters: introduction, literature review, method, lexical comparison (Swadesh list, initialisation, ASL influence), word-order comparison, conclusion. The only 'phonology' is the four sign parameters (handshape, location, orientation, movement) used as the criterion for identical/similar/different signs (pp. 16, 23). Prosody appears only negatively: no non-manual topicalisation marker such as 'intonational break, raised eyebrows, or head-tilt' was observed in object-first Jakarta sentences (p. 53) and 'no significant prosodic feature is observed as a topicalizati…

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid pages indo1291 (Jakartan Sign Language) and indo1333 (Indonesian Sign, pseudo-family); Wikipedia 'Indonesian Sign Language' (raw wikitext)
sources.note: Glottolog lists only Hurlbut 2003/2014 lexicostatistics and Sze 2021; Wikipedia cites only Isma 2012 and says nothing about phonology or prosody.

sources.access_detail: open copy online, not fetched sources
sources.note: The published, revised form of the 2015 thesis already read; the most authoritative description of any BISINDO variety (Solo, Makassar). Open access but De Gruyter's site returns a bot challenge (HTTP 202, empty body) to automated fetch and 405 to web lookups; DOAB record 20.500.12854/132928 holds no PDF. Not expected to add a stress statement, but would supersede the thesis for citation.

sources.citation: Sukmara, Galuh. 2014. [Phonological components of the Yogyakarta variety of Indonesian Sign Language] (as cited in Palfreyman 2015, p. 18: 'Sukmara (2014) explores phonological components').

sources.note: The only phonological study of a Javanese BISINDO variety named in the literature; Yogyakarta rather than Jakarta (Glottolog treats them as distinct), so any prosodic statement would need an identity note.

sources.citation: Hurlbut, Hope M. 2013. The signed languages of Indonesia: An enigma. SIL International report, 20 pp. (Glottolog cites it as Hurlbut 2014).
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Lexicostatistical rapid survey of 21 urban sign varieties including Jakarta; establishes the variety inventory and naming but not phonology. Not located on sil.

sources.citation: Suwiryo, Adhika Irlang. 2013. Mouth movement patterns in Jakarta and Yogyakarta Sign Language: A preliminary study. MA thesis, Chinese University of Hong Kong.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Only Jakarta-specific study of a non-manual (mouthing/mouth gesture) channel, the channel that carries prosodic prominence in sign languages; the nearest thing to a prosodic description of JakSL. Not in the Wayback listing of the CUHK MA-papers directory.
